fullPassage: The history of the distinction between the second person pronouns 'thou' and 'you' is a revealing example of how language change relates to social change. The Oxford English Dictionary tells us that early forms of 'thou' (plus 'thee', 'thine', and 'thy') and 'you' (plus 'ye', 'your', and 'yours') were both used in ordinary speech in Old English, where the distinction was primarily a grammatical one. In Middle English, 'you' began to be used as a mark of respect when addressing a superior and (later) an equal, while 'thou' was retained for addressing an inferior. This distinction between 'thou' and 'you' was related to the strict stratification of society in the Middle Ages. It allowed an aristocratic speaker to distinguish between an equal (referred to as 'you') and someone inferior in social standing (referred to as 'thou'), or to signal intimacy. The lower orders, on the other hand, were required to address aristocrats as 'you' as a mark of deference. In the fifteenth century, the rising merchant classes began using 'thou' to the lower orders. Increasing social mobility and competition between this merchant class and the aristocracy meant that by Shakespeare's time there was widespread confusion about who should use the term 'thou' to whom. The seventeenth-century radical Quaker movement seized on the confusion about 'thou' and 'you' by using 'thou' to everyone, as a political act of levelling. The distinction eventually collapsed, and only 'you' survived. 'Thou' only appears now in archaizing registers, including those of poetry and religion, where it functions, curiously enough, as a marker of respect rather than of inferiority.

questions.stem:
주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.

The history of the distinction between the second person pronouns 'thou' and 'you' is a revealing example of how language change relates to social change.

(A) In the fifteenth century, the rising merchant classes began using 'thou' to the lower orders. Increasing social mobility and competition between this merchant class and the aristocracy meant that by Shakespeare's time there was widespread confusion about who should use the term 'thou' to whom.

(B) The seventeenth-century radical Quaker movement seized on the confusion about 'thou' and 'you' by using 'thou' to everyone, as a political act of levelling. The distinction eventually collapsed, and only 'you' survived.

(C) In Middle English, 'you' began to be used as a mark of respect when addressing a superior and (later) an equal, while 'thou' was retained for addressing an inferior. The lower orders, on the other hand, were required to address aristocrats as 'you' as a mark of deference.

det.korean: 'thou'와 'you'라는 2인칭 대명사 구분의 역사는 언어 변화가 사회 변화와 어떻게 관련되는지를 보여주는 흥미로운 예이다. (C) 중세 영어에서 'you'는 윗사람과 (나중에는) 동등한 사람을 부를 때 존중의 표시로 쓰이기 시작했고, 'thou'는 아랫사람을 부를 때 남아 있었다. 반면 하류층은 귀족에게 존경의 표시로 'you'라고 부르도록 요구받았다. (A) 15세기에 떠오르는 상인 계층은 하류층에게 'thou'를 사용하기 시작했다. 상인 계층과 귀족 사이의 사회적 이동성과 경쟁 증가로, 셰익스피어 시대에는 누가 누구에게 'thou'를 써야 하는지에 대한 widespread한 혼란이 있었다. (B) 17세기의 급진적인 퀘이커 운동은 모든 사람에게 'thou'를 사용함으로써 이 혼란을 정치적 평등화 행위로 이용했다. 그 구분은 결국 붕괴되었고 오직 'you'만 남았다.
det.analysis:
① (A)-(B)-(C) ❌: 주어진 글은 아직 신분에 따른 thou/you 구분(중세 영어)을 소개하지 않았는데, (A)에서 바로 '상인 계층의 thou 사용'이 나오면 비교 대상이 없어 흐름이 끊긴다.

② (A)-(C)-(B) ❌: (A)의 '혼란(confusion)'이 설명되기도 전에 상인 계층의 행동만 먼저 나오고, 그 뒤에야 (C)의 신분제 규칙이 나오는 것은 원인(신분제)보다 결과(혼란)가 앞서는 부자연스러운 순서다.

③ (B)-(C)-(A) ❌: (B)의 퀘이커 운동과 구분의 소멸이 먼저 나오면, 아직 설명되지 않은 '상인 계층의 등장(A)'과 '신분제 규칙(C)'을 전제로 한 내용이 뒤에 나와 시간 순서가 거꾸로 된다.

④ (C)-(A)-(B) ✅: 주어진 글(고대 영어의 문법적 구분) 다음에 (C)에서 중세 영어의 신분제적 구분(존경-you, 하위-thou)이 확립됨을 설명하고, (A)에서 15세기 상인 계층이 이 규칙에 혼란을 일으키기 시작했음을, (B)에서 17세기 퀘이커 운동과 구분의 소멸, 현재의 용법까지 시간 순서대로 이어지므로 가장 적절하다 ←정답
det.tip: 시간을 나타내는 표현(Middle English → the fifteenth century → the seventeenth century)을 추적하면 순서를 쉽게 찾을 수 있다.

④ — 이 위치는 이미 'widespread confusion(혼란)'까지 진행된 뒤이므로, '무너지기 시작했다'는 주어진 문장이 오히려 이야기를 거꾸로 되돌리게 된다.

It allowed an aristocratic speaker to distinguish between an equal (referred to as 'you') and someone inferior in social standing (referred to as 'thou'), or to signal intimacy. ① The lower orders, on the other hand, were required to address aristocrats as 'you' as a mark of deference. ② In the fifteenth century, the rising merchant classes began using 'thou' to the lower orders. ③ Many online discussion forums today debate whether people should use formal or informal pronouns when texting friends. ④ Increasing social mobility and competition between this merchant class and the aristocracy meant that by Shakespeare's time there was widespread confusion about who should use the term 'thou' to whom. The seventeenth-century radical Quaker movement seized on the confusion about 'thou' and 'you' by using 'thou' to everyone, as a political act of levelling. The distinction eventually collapsed, and only 'you' survived. 'Thou' only appears now in archaizing registers, including those of poetry and religion, where it functions, curiously enough, as a marker of respect rather than of inferiority.
